title: Antimycobacterial, Antifungal & Antiparasitic Drugs
summary: TB regimens, antifungal targets and antiparasitic drugs.

lessons.title: Tuberculosis Drugs

levels.kid:
**Tuberculosis**, or TB, is caused by a slow, stubborn germ that often hides in the lungs. It wears a thick, waxy coat, like a raincoat that keeps medicine out.

One medicine alone isn't enough. Some TB germs might be tough against one medicine, so doctors use **four medicines together** at the start. It's like having four locks on a door: the germ can't pick them all.

Treatment takes many months because the germ grows so slowly. Taking every pill, every time, is what beats it. One TB medicine even turns tears and pee orange!
levels.hs:
**Tuberculosis** is caused by ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***, a slow-growing bacterium with a thick, waxy **mycolic acid** cell wall. It can hide inside immune cells and in walled-off lung lesions.

**Why combination therapy?** In a large TB population, a few bacteria are naturally resistant to any one drug. With **several drugs at once**, a germ would need resistance to all of them, which is extremely unlikely. Treatment is also long (usually at least **6 months**) because some bacteria are dormant and grow very slowly.

**The first-line drugs ("RIPE"):**
- **Rifampin:** blocks bacterial RNA polymerase. Turns urine, sweat and tears **orange-red**. Speeds up the liver's breakdown of many other drugs (birth control, blood thinners, HIV drugs).
- **Isoniazid:** blocks mycolic acid synthesis. Can cause **liver injury** and **nerve damage**; vitamin **B6 (pyridoxine)** prevents the nerve damage.
- **Pyrazinamide:** works best in the acidic environment where dormant TB hides. Can cause liver injury and raise **uric acid** (gout).
- **Ethambutol:** blocks another cell wall component. Can damage the **optic nerve**, so vision (especially red-green color vision) is checked.

**Latent TB** (infection without disease) is treated with fewer drugs to prevent future illness.

**Drug-resistant TB** (**MDR-TB** resists isoniazid and rifampin) needs newer drugs like **bedaquiline**, **pretomanid** and **linezolid**.
levels.college:
**Mycobacterial biology shapes therapy.** The envelope (peptidoglycan–arabinogalactan–mycolic acid complex) limits drug entry; doubling time is roughly a day; populations differ: rapidly growing extracellular bacilli in cavities, slowly metabolizing bacilli in acidic caseum and macrophages, and near-dormant persisters. Each drug kills a different subpopulation, and combinations prevent the selection of spontaneous resistant mutants.

**First-line agents:**
- **Isoniazid (INH):** prodrug activated by catalase-peroxidase **KatG** to an isonicotinoyl radical that forms an adduct with NAD, inhibiting **InhA** (enoyl-ACP reductase, FAS-II) and blocking **mycolic acid** synthesis. Bactericidal for dividing cells; the main early killer. Metabolized by **NAT2** acetylation (slow acetylators have higher levels, more toxicity). Toxicity: **hepatitis** (age-related), **peripheral neuropathy** (pyridoxine depletion: INH forms hydrazones with pyridoxal and inhibits pyridoxine kinase), drug-induced lupus, CYP2C19/3A4 inhibition (raises phenytoin).
- **Rifampin:** binds the β-subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (**rpoB**), blocking elongation; sterilizing activity against semi-dormant bacilli. Potent **PXR-mediated inducer** of CYP3A4, 2C9, 2C19, UGTs and P-gp. Orange body fluids, hepatitis, flu-like syndrome, thrombocytopenia. **Rifabutin** induces less (preferred with HIV protease inhibitors); **rifapentine** has a long half-life.
- **Pyrazinamide:** prodrug converted by **pyrazinamidase (pncA)** to pyrazinoic acid, active at acidic pH; proposed targets include PanD (coenzyme A synthesis). Sterilizing; allows shortening to 6 months. Hepatotoxicity, **hyperuricemia** (inhibits urate secretion), arthralgia.
- **Ethambutol:** inhibits **arabinosyltransferases (embB)**, blocking arabinogalactan. Bacteriostatic; protects against resistance. **Optic neuritis** (reduced acuity, red-green color loss), renally cleared.

**Regimen logic:** an intensive phase with four drugs followed by a continuation phase with INH and rifampin. **Directly observed therapy** improves adherence. A 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen is an alternative for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB.

**Resistance:** INH via **katG** (high-level) or **inhA** promoter (low-level, cross-resistance to ethionamide); rifampin via **rpoB** mutations (detected rapidly by molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF). **MDR-TB**: INH + rifampin resistance; regimens such as **BPaLM** (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) now shorten treatment. **Bedaquiline** inhibits mycobacterial **ATP synthase** (c subunit; QT prolongation). **Pretomanid** is a nitroimidazole prodrug activated by Ddn.
levels.phd:
**Why TB therapy takes months.** Mathematical and animal (e.g., Cornell model, rabbit caseum) studies show that the bulk of bacilli die early, but a phenotypically tolerant fraction in caseous necrosis and macrophages dies slowly. Caseum is a lipid-rich, acellular, near-neutral-to-mildly acidic, hypoxic environment; drugs differ dramatically in caseum penetration and in binding to caseum macromolecules (Dartois's lesion-PK work by MALDI imaging showed rifampin and pyrazinamide penetrate well, while moxifloxacin accumulates in cellular rims and bedaquiline binds tightly to caseum). This **lesion pharmacokinetics** explains why plasma levels poorly predict sterilization and why some regimens with good early bactericidal activity fail to shorten therapy.

**Isoniazid activation chemistry.** KatG oxidizes INH to an isonicotinoyl radical that couples with NAD⁺ to form an INH-NAD adduct, a slow, tight-binding InhA inhibitor. The **katG S315T** substitution preserves catalase-peroxidase function (needed against host oxidative stress) while impairing INH activation: an elegant evolutionary compromise accounting for most high-level resistance. Direct InhA inhibitors that bypass KatG are in development.

**Pyrazinamide's enigma.** The drug was found empirically and its mechanism remained obscure for decades; proposals included membrane energetics disruption by protonated pyrazinoic acid, trans-translation (RpsA) and, best supported now, degradation of **PanD** triggered by pyrazinoic acid binding, depleting coenzyme A. Resistance arises mainly through scattered *pncA* loss-of-function mutations, complicating molecular diagnosis.

**Bedaquiline** binds the c-ring of the F₀ rotor, stalling proton translocation; it also uncouples electron transport. Its very long terminal half-life (from adipose accumulation) leaves a resistance-prone "tail" after stopping. Resistance via **Rv0678** mutations (MmpS5–MmpL5 efflux upregulation) also lowers clofazimine susceptibility. **Pretomanid** under hypoxia releases reactive nitrogen species (nitric oxide), killing non-replicating bacilli, and under aerobic conditions inhibits mycolic acid synthesis.

**Host-directed therapy** (e.g., modulating eicosanoid balance, matrix metalloproteinases, or adjunctive corticosteroids in TB meningitis) aims to limit immunopathology rather than kill bacilli.
levels.expert:
**Tuberculous meningitis is the neurosurgeon's TB problem.** It presents subacutely with headache, fever, cranial nerve palsies (especially CN VI), and basal meningeal enhancement on MRI; complications include **communicating hydrocephalus** (often needing a ventricular drain or shunt), vasculitic infarcts in the basal ganglia and internal capsule, and tuberculomas. Treatment uses the standard four drugs for an extended course, with **adjunctive dexamethasone**, which reduces mortality in HIV-negative adults. Rifampin's CSF penetration is limited, so higher-intensity rifampin regimens are being studied. **Paradoxical reactions** (worsening lesions after starting therapy, especially with immune reconstitution in HIV) may need steroids or surgery rather than a regimen change. **Spinal TB (Pott disease)** may need decompression and stabilization for cord compression or instability.

**Toxicity management in practice:**
- **Hepatotoxicity:** baseline liver tests in at-risk patients, symptoms monitoring for all. If transaminases rise substantially with symptoms, stop the hepatotoxic drugs and reintroduce one by one.
- **Pyridoxine** for patients at risk of neuropathy (diabetes, alcohol use disorder, HIV, pregnancy, malnutrition, kidney disease).
- **Monthly vision and color checks** on ethambutol, especially with renal impairment.
- **Rifampin interactions** are the most common source of harm: warfarin, DOACs, antiseizure drugs, tacrolimus, hormonal contraception, corticosteroids (reduced effect, relevant to TB meningitis steroid choices) and many antiretrovirals. Plan the whole medication list before starting.

**Diagnosis-driven choices:** molecular testing for rifampin resistance at diagnosis determines the regimen from day one; phenotypic and sequencing-based susceptibility testing follow.

**Nontuberculous mycobacteria:** *M. avium* complex is treated with a macrolide, ethambutol and a rifamycin; *M. abscessus* is notoriously drug-resistant.

**Leprosy:** multidrug therapy with dapsone, rifampin and clofazimine.

keyPoints: TB needs combination therapy to prevent resistance and long courses to kill slow and dormant bacilli
RIPE: rifampin (rpoB; orange fluids; CYP inducer), isoniazid (KatG-activated; InhA; neuropathy prevented by B6), pyrazinamide (acidic pH; hyperuricemia), ethambutol (embB; optic neuritis)
MDR-TB = resistance to isoniazid and rifampin; newer drugs: bedaquiline (ATP synthase), pretomanid, linezolid
Isoniazid resistance mainly katG S315T; rifampin resistance via rpoB mutations
TB meningitis: four drugs plus adjunctive dexamethasone; watch for hydrocephalus

lessons.title: Azoles and Polyenes

levels.kid:
**Fungi** are living things like mold and yeast. Some can cause infections, from itchy feet to serious lung or brain infections.

Fungi are more like our own cells than bacteria are, so it's harder to find medicine that hurts them but not us.

One trick: fungi use a special fat called **ergosterol** in their skin. We use a different one.

**Azoles** stop fungi from making ergosterol. **Amphotericin** grabs ergosterol and pokes holes in the fungus. Amphotericin is very strong but can be rough on the kidneys, so doctors watch closely.
levels.hs:
Fungal cells are **eukaryotic** like ours, so selective targets are fewer. The main one is **ergosterol**, the sterol in fungal membranes (human cells use **cholesterol**).

**Azoles** block **lanosterol 14α-demethylase**, an enzyme fungi need to make ergosterol. Without it, the membrane becomes faulty.
- **Fluconazole:** yeast (*Candida*) and ***Cryptococcus*** infections; gets into the brain and spinal fluid well.
- **Itraconazole:** fungi found in certain regions, like *Histoplasma* and *Blastomyces*.
- **Voriconazole:** first choice for ***Aspergillus*** (a mold that infects lungs of people with weak immunity). Can cause **vision changes** and sun sensitivity.
- **Posaconazole** and **isavuconazole:** broad, including *Mucor*-type molds.
- **Topical azoles** (clotrimazole, miconazole): athlete's foot, skin and yeast infections.
Azoles also block human liver enzymes (CYP3A4), causing many **drug interactions**, and some affect heart rhythm.

**Polyenes:**
- **Amphotericin B** binds ergosterol and makes **pores** in the membrane, killing the fungus. It is very broad and used for severe infections like **cryptococcal meningitis** and mucormycosis. Side effects: fever and chills during infusion, **kidney damage**, low potassium and magnesium. **Lipid (liposomal)** forms are gentler on the kidneys.
- **Nystatin** is too toxic for the bloodstream, so it's used on skin or swished in the mouth for thrush.
levels.college:
**Ergosterol biosynthesis:** squalene → (squalene epoxidase; terbinafine) → lanosterol → (**CYP51/Erg11, 14α-demethylase**; azoles) → … → ergosterol. Azole nitrogen (imidazole N3 or triazole N4) coordinates the **heme iron** of CYP51, blocking demethylation; ergosterol depletion and accumulation of toxic **14α-methylated sterols** disrupt membrane function. Azoles are **fungistatic against yeasts** and fungicidal against some molds.

**Agents:**
- **Fluconazole:** water-soluble, high oral bioavailability, renal excretion, excellent CSF and urine levels. Gaps: no mold activity; *C. krusei* intrinsically resistant; *C. glabrata* (Nakaseomyces glabratus) often reduced susceptibility; *C. auris* frequently resistant.
- **Itraconazole:** variable absorption (capsule needs acid and food; solution better), negative inotropy (avoid in heart failure).
- **Voriconazole:** *Aspergillus* first-line; nonlinear PK and **CYP2C19 polymorphism** require therapeutic drug monitoring. Toxicity: transient **visual disturbances** (retinal), hallucinations, hepatotoxicity, phototoxicity and **squamous cell carcinoma** with long use, **periostitis** (fluoride excess), QT prolongation.
- **Posaconazole:** activity against Mucorales; prophylaxis in leukemia and transplant.
- **Isavuconazole:** Mucorales and *Aspergillus*; **shortens** the QT interval; fewer interactions.
- **Ketoconazole:** systemic use largely abandoned (hepatotoxicity); inhibits adrenal steroidogenesis (used for Cushing syndrome).

All azoles inhibit **CYP3A4** (strongly: ketoconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole; fluconazole moderately, also CYP2C9/2C19), raising tacrolimus, cyclosporine, vincristine (neuropathy), statins and midazolam.

**Amphotericin B:** amphipathic polyene; binds ergosterol preferentially over cholesterol; fungicidal. **Toxicity:** infusion-related fever and rigors (TLR2/CD14-mediated cytokine release), **nephrotoxicity** (afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction plus distal tubular damage) causing **hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia**, distal (type 1) RTA; normocytic anemia (reduced erythropoietin). Mitigation: saline loading, lipid formulations (liposomal, lipid complex). Poor CSF levels yet effective in cryptococcal meningitis, combined with **flucytosine**.

**Resistance:** ERG11 point mutations and overexpression, efflux pumps (CDR1/CDR2 ABC transporters, MDR1 MFS transporter), and in *Aspergillus* the **TR34/L98H** cyp51A alteration linked to agricultural azole fungicides.
levels.phd:
**How amphotericin really kills.** The classic model held that amphotericin assembles into barrel-stave ion channels with ergosterol. Burke's group showed in 2014 that channel formation is not required for killing: a derivative unable to form channels (C35-deoxy) still kills, and amphotericin primarily forms large extramembranous **sterol sponge** aggregates that extract ergosterol from membranes. This reframed toxicity as differential extraction of ergosterol versus cholesterol and enabled rational design of **AM-2-19** and related derivatives that bind ergosterol but not cholesterol, retaining fungicidal activity with much less renal toxicity in animals.

**CYP51 structural pharmacology.** Long-tailed triazoles (itraconazole, posaconazole) extend through the substrate access channel, making contacts that confer mold activity and resistance robustness; short azoles (fluconazole, voriconazole) are more vulnerable to single substitutions. Selectivity over human CYP51 is modest at the heme but supplemented by differences in the access channel; tetrazoles (**oteseconazole**) bind heme more weakly, improving selectivity and lowering human CYP inhibition.

**Resistance through stress tolerance.** Azole exposure induces ERG gene upregulation via Upc2 and efflux via Tac1 and Mrr1 gain-of-function mutations; *Candida albicans* rapidly gains **aneuploidy** (isochromosome 5L carrying ERG11 and TAC1) as a fast, reversible resistance route. The **calcineurin and Hsp90** stress pathways are required for azole tolerance; their inhibitors turn fungistatic azoles fungicidal in vitro, a target for combination strategies.

**One Health dimension.** Environmental *Aspergillus fumigatus* with tandem promoter repeats (TR34/L98H, TR46/Y121F/T289A) arise from agricultural demethylation-inhibitor fungicides structurally similar to medical azoles; patients can present with azole-resistant infection without prior azole exposure.

**Candida auris** emerged near-simultaneously on several continents around 2009–2016 as separate clades, with frequent fluconazole resistance (Erg11 substitutions), variable amphotericin resistance and persistence on surfaces, making it a hospital infection-control problem as much as a drug problem.
levels.expert:
**Neurological fungal infections an attending sees:**
- **Cryptococcal meningitis** (advanced HIV, transplant): induction with **liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine**, then consolidation and maintenance with fluconazole. Raised intracranial pressure is a major killer: manage with **repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures**, and a shunt if pressure stays high despite that. Steroids worsen outcomes here and are not used. Antiretroviral therapy is delayed several weeks after starting antifungals to reduce fatal immune reconstitution.
- **Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis** (diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia): emergency **surgical debridement plus liposomal amphotericin B**; isavuconazole or posaconazole for step-down. Voriconazole has no Mucorales activity, and breakthrough mucormycosis on voriconazole prophylaxis is a known trap.
- **CNS aspergillosis:** voriconazole, which penetrates the brain well, plus surgical excision where possible.

**Practical pharmacology:**
- **Therapeutic drug monitoring** for voriconazole, posaconazole and itraconazole; CYP2C19 genotype guides voriconazole.
- **Interaction review is mandatory:** azoles raise tacrolimus and cyclosporine (preemptive dose reduction in transplant), vincristine (severe neuropathy, so avoid azoles near vincristine), certain statins, and some antiseizure drugs; conversely, rifampin, carbamazepine and phenytoin can make azole levels useless.
- **QT:** combine ECG monitoring with electrolyte correction; isavuconazole is a QT-friendly choice.
- **Amphotericin:** pre-hydrate with saline, replace potassium and magnesium aggressively, monitor creatinine; premedication helps infusion reactions. Use lipid formulations for CNS disease and anyone at kidney risk.
- Long-term voriconazole users need dermatologic surveillance and sun protection (skin cancer), and bone pain prompts checking fluoride.

**Candida:** fluconazole remains excellent for susceptible species, but species and susceptibility drive step-down from echinocandin therapy; *C. auris* requires infection-control notification.

keyPoints: Ergosterol is the main selective fungal target; human cells use cholesterol
Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51/Erg11); fungistatic against yeasts
Fluconazole: Candida, Cryptococcus, good CSF; voriconazole: Aspergillus (visual changes, phototoxicity); posaconazole/isavuconazole: Mucorales
Azoles inhibit CYP3A4 → interactions (tacrolimus, vincristine); most prolong QT, isavuconazole shortens it
Amphotericin B binds ergosterol (sterol sponge/pores); toxicity: infusion reactions, nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia; lipid forms reduce it

lessons.title: Echinocandins and Other Antifungals

levels.kid:
Fungi have a wall, kind of like bacteria, but it's built from different stuff. One important brick is called **glucan**.

**Echinocandins** stop fungi from making glucan bricks, so the wall falls apart. Our cells don't have that wall, so these medicines are gentle on us. They're great for yeast infections in the blood.

**Terbinafine** helps with fungus in toenails and skin.

**Flucytosine** is a sneaky one: only the fungus turns it into poison, but it works best with a buddy medicine so the fungus can't get used to it.
levels.hs:
**Echinocandins** (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin, and the newer **rezafungin**) block **β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase**, the enzyme that makes a key **fungal cell wall** polysaccharide. Humans have no such wall, so these drugs are very well tolerated.
- **First choice for *Candida* bloodstream infections** (candidemia), especially in sick ICU patients.
- Also used for *Aspergillus* when other drugs fail.
- Given **IV only**.
- **Don't work on *Cryptococcus*** and get poorly into the **brain** and urine.

**Other antifungals:**
- **Flucytosine (5-FC):** fungi convert it into **5-fluorouracil**, which blocks DNA and RNA building. Humans can't convert it much. Fungi become resistant quickly if it's used alone, so it's combined with **amphotericin B** for cryptococcal meningitis. It can lower blood counts.
- **Terbinafine:** blocks **squalene epoxidase**, an early ergosterol step. Treats **nail and skin fungus** (dermatophytes) and builds up in nails. Can rarely affect the liver and taste.
- **Griseofulvin:** an older drug that stops fungal cell division; deposits in hair and skin; used for scalp ringworm in children.

***Pneumocystis***, a fungus that causes pneumonia in people with weak immune systems, lacks ergosterol, so it's treated with **TMP-SMX** instead of usual antifungals.
levels.college:
**Echinocandins.** Lipopeptides that noncompetitively inhibit the catalytic **Fks** subunit of β-(1,3)-glucan synthase (regulated by Rho1). Loss of glucan causes osmotic fragility. **Fungicidal** against most *Candida*; **fungistatic** against *Aspergillus*, where they cause aberrant, blunted hyphal tips. Inactive against *Cryptococcus* (glucan synthase relatively insensitive; capsule) and Mucorales, and against *Fusarium*/*Scedosporium* in practice.
- **PK:** large lipopeptides, IV only, highly protein-bound, hepatic or nonenzymatic degradation, no renal adjustment, minimal CSF, urine and eye penetration (poor for CNS candidiasis, endophthalmitis or cystitis). **Rezafungin** has a very long half-life permitting infrequent administration.
- **Toxicity:** low; histamine-like infusion reactions, mild hepatic enzyme rises; caspofungin interacts with cyclosporine and inducers.
- **Resistance:** hot-spot mutations in **FKS1** (and **FKS2** in *C. glabrata*); more common in *C. glabrata* and *C. auris*. *C. parapsilosis* has a naturally higher MIC.

**Flucytosine:** taken up by cytosine permease (Fcy2), deaminated by **cytosine deaminase** (Fcy1, absent in mammals) to **5-FU**, then converted to 5-FUTP (incorporated into RNA) and 5-FdUMP (inhibits **thymidylate synthase**). Rapid resistance (permease, deaminase or UPRT mutations) mandates combination. Renally cleared; toxicity is concentration-related **myelosuppression**, hepatitis and enterocolitis, partly from gut bacterial conversion to 5-FU; level monitoring is advised.

**Allylamines:** **terbinafine** inhibits squalene epoxidase (Erg1) noncompetitively; squalene accumulation is fungicidal for dermatophytes. Lipophilic, concentrates in keratin. Adverse: rare severe hepatotoxicity, taste and smell disturbance, CYP2D6 inhibition (raises some antidepressants and β-blockers).

**Griseofulvin:** binds tubulin, disrupting the mitotic spindle; deposited in keratin precursor cells. CYP inducer (reduces warfarin, contraceptives), teratogenic, photosensitivity.

**Newer agents:** **ibrexafungerp** (oral triterpenoid glucan synthase inhibitor, different binding site from echinocandins); **fosmanogepix** (inhibits Gwt1, GPI-anchor biosynthesis); **olorofim** (orotomide inhibiting fungal **dihydroorotate dehydrogenase**, active against *Aspergillus* and *Scedosporium* but not yeasts).
levels.phd:
**Glucan synthase structure.** Cryo-EM structures of *Saccharomyces* Fks1 (2023) revealed a membrane-embedded glycosyltransferase with a transmembrane channel through which the nascent glucan chain is extruded. The echinocandin resistance hot spots map near a lipid-facing region adjacent to the channel, implying that echinocandins act at the membrane–protein interface, consistent with their lipophilic tails; ergosterol and sphingolipid composition modulate susceptibility, explaining why membrane lipid changes alter echinocandin MICs without Fks mutations.

**Paradoxical (Eagle-like) effect.** Some *Candida* and *Aspergillus* isolates grow better at very high echinocandin concentrations, through compensatory **chitin** synthesis driven by the PKC, HOG and calcineurin cell-wall integrity pathways. Chitin-rich cells are less susceptible, and combining echinocandins with chitin synthase inhibitors (nikkomycin Z) or calcineurin inhibitors abolishes this in vitro.

**Immunological unmasking.** Echinocandins expose β-glucan normally hidden under the mannoprotein layer, increasing recognition by **Dectin-1** on macrophages and neutrophils, so part of their in vivo efficacy may be immune-mediated, not purely cell-autonomous.

**Flucytosine's comeback.** Large African trials (ACTA, AMBITION-cm) showed that flucytosine-containing combinations, including a single high-intensity liposomal amphotericin induction with flucytosine and fluconazole, reduced cryptococcal meningitis mortality compared with older regimens, establishing it as essential despite limited global availability. Faster CSF fungal clearance (early fungicidal activity) predicted survival.

**New targets beyond the membrane.** Gwt1 inhibition by manogepix blocks inositol acylation in GPI-anchor synthesis, preventing cell wall mannoprotein display. Olorofim exploits structural differences between fungal and human DHODH, a target previously used in human immunology (leflunomide/teriflunomide), illustrating how the same enzyme can be selectively hit across kingdoms. These agents matter because they bypass all existing azole, polyene and echinocandin resistance.
levels.expert:
**Candidemia playbook.** Start an **echinocandin** for candidemia in most hospitalized patients; remove central venous catheters when feasible; obtain a **dilated eye exam** (endophthalmitis changes duration and drug choice because echinocandins don't reach the eye well); repeat blood cultures until clear; treat for a defined period after the first negative culture. Step down to fluconazole when the patient is stable and the isolate is susceptible. *C. auris* requires echinocandin therapy with infection-control isolation.

**CNS caveats.** Echinocandins should not be relied upon for *Candida* meningitis, ventriculitis or shunt infection; liposomal amphotericin B (with or without flucytosine) followed by fluconazole is preferred, and an infected shunt or drain should be removed. Neonatal candidiasis frequently involves the CNS, which is why amphotericin or fluconazole, not echinocandins, are standard there.

**Cryptococcal meningitis:** flucytosine is a crucial partner. Watch blood counts and, where available, levels, especially with renal impairment; reduce exposure as kidney function falls.

**Dermatophytes:** terbinafine is first-line for toenail onychomycosis (long courses because nails grow slowly); confirm the diagnosis with microscopy or culture first because many "fungal nails" aren't. Check liver tests in those with liver disease and advise stopping for jaundice, dark urine or fatigue. Griseofulvin remains used for tinea capitis in children.

**Prophylaxis strategies:** in high-risk hematology patients, mold-active azoles are preferred; echinocandins are used when azoles can't be given because of interactions (e.g., with vincristine or venetoclax).

**Pitfalls:** echinocandins for *Candida* urinary infection (poor urine levels); assuming a *C. parapsilosis* line infection will clear with an echinocandin (higher MICs, fluconazole often preferred); and missing *Cryptococcus* in a patient on echinocandin prophylaxis, since they provide no coverage.

**Biomarkers:** serum β-D-glucan supports invasive fungal diagnosis but is negative in cryptococcosis and mucormycosis and false-positive with some IV products.

keyPoints: Echinocandins inhibit β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase (Fks1); fungicidal for Candida, fungistatic for Aspergillus

Flucytosine → 5-FU in fungi (cytosine deaminase); combined with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis; myelosuppression
Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase (dermatophytes, nails); griseofulvin binds tubulin
Newer targets: Gwt1 (fosmanogepix), fungal DHODH (olorofim), oral glucan synthase inhibitor (ibrexafungerp)

lessons.title: Antimalarials

levels.kid:
**Malaria** is caused by a tiny parasite that mosquitoes carry. When a mosquito bites, the parasite goes first to the **liver** to hide and multiply, then into the **blood**, where it breaks into red blood cells.

Different medicines attack the parasite in different hiding spots.

Some medicines, like **artemisinin**, which came from a plant used in old Chinese medicine, attack it fast in the blood. Others clean out sleeping parasites left in the liver so the sickness doesn't come back.

Travelers can take medicine before a trip to help stop malaria from starting.
levels.hs:
**Malaria** is caused by ***Plasmodium*** parasites spread by *Anopheles* mosquitoes. *P. falciparum* is the most dangerous; it can cause **cerebral malaria** (brain swelling, coma, seizures).

**Life cycle and drug targets:**
- **Liver stage:** parasites multiply in liver cells. *P. vivax* and *P. ovale* can leave dormant **hypnozoites** that cause relapses months later.
- **Blood stage:** parasites invade red blood cells and digest **hemoglobin**. This causes the fevers and is where most drugs act.

**Drug classes:**
- **Artemisinins** (artesunate, artemether): very fast-acting blood-stage killers. Given in **artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs)**, such as artemether-lumefantrine, to prevent resistance. **IV artesunate** is the treatment for severe malaria.
- **Chloroquine:** stops the parasite from safely disposing of toxic heme. Much *P. falciparum* is now resistant, but it still works for some other species in some regions.
- **Primaquine and tafenoquine:** kill **hypnozoites** ("radical cure"). They can cause dangerous hemolysis in **G6PD deficiency**, so testing comes first.
- **Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine:** used for **prevention** in travelers. Mefloquine can cause neuropsychiatric side effects.
- **Quinine:** older drug; can cause ringing in the ears and low blood sugar.

The discovery of artemisinin by **Tu Youyou** won the 2015 Nobel Prize.
levels.college:
**Blood-stage biology:** trophozoites endocytose hemoglobin into an acidic **digestive vacuole**; proteolysis releases free **heme** (ferriprotoporphyrin IX), which is toxic, so the parasite crystallizes it into inert **hemozoin**.

**Agents:**
- **Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (4-aminoquinolines):** weak bases trapped by protonation in the acidic vacuole; bind heme and **block hemozoin formation**, so toxic heme accumulates. Resistance: **PfCRT** mutations (K76T) that export drug from the vacuole; PfMDR1 modulates. Adverse: pruritus, QT prolongation, retinopathy with long-term use, hypoglycemia, neuropsychiatric effects, myopathy.
- **Quinine/quinidine (aryl-amino alcohols):** similar mechanism; **cinchonism** (tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, visual changes), **hypoglycemia** (stimulates insulin release), QT prolongation.
- **Mefloquine:** blood schizonticide; long half-life; **neuropsychiatric** adverse effects (boxed: anxiety, depression, psychosis, vestibular symptoms that can persist), avoid with seizure or psychiatric history.
- **Lumefantrine, piperaquine, amodiaquine:** long-acting ACT partners that clear residual parasites after the artemisinin.
- **Artemisinins:** the **endoperoxide bridge** is cleaved by ferrous heme iron, generating carbon-centered radicals that **alkylate many parasite proteins** and heme. Very rapid parasite clearance, short half-life (hence partner drugs). Active on young ring stages, which prevents sequestration. Adverse: generally safe; **post-artesunate delayed hemolysis** after severe malaria. Partial resistance (delayed clearance) from **kelch13** mutations, first in Southeast Asia and now independently in East Africa.
- **Atovaquone:** inhibits mitochondrial **cytochrome bc1**, collapsing membrane potential and blocking pyrimidine synthesis (DHODH depends on it). **Proguanil** is metabolized (CYP2C19) to **cycloguanil**, a DHFR inhibitor, and also synergizes with atovaquone directly. Active on liver and blood stages, used for prophylaxis and treatment.
- **Pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine:** antifolate combination; intermittent preventive therapy in pregnancy and seasonal chemoprevention.
- **8-aminoquinolines (primaquine, tafenoquine):** kill **hypnozoites** and **gametocytes** (blocking transmission). Mechanism involves CYP2D6 metabolites generating reactive oxygen species. **Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency**; contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal G6PD status unknown). Poor CYP2D6 metabolizers respond less to primaquine.
levels.phd:
**The artemisinin story and its biology.** Project 523, a Chinese military program launched in 1967, screened traditional remedies; Tu Youyou's team found that a low-temperature ether extraction of *Artemisia annua* (inspired by a 4th-century text by Ge Hong describing cold water soaking) preserved activity destroyed by hot extraction. The pharmacophore is the 1,2,4-trioxane endoperoxide.

Chemical proteomics (Wang and colleagues, 2015) showed that activated artemisinin alkylates over a hundred parasite proteins, and its activation is heme-dependent, which explains selectivity for hemoglobin-digesting stages. Partial resistance through **kelch13** mutations does not change the IC50 in standard assays; instead, mutant ring-stage parasites reduce hemoglobin endocytosis (K13 is part of an endocytosis complex), lowering heme-mediated activation, and display an enhanced unfolded-protein and proteasome stress response. Hence the **ring-stage survival assay** rather than conventional IC50 is used to measure it. Combining artemisinins with proteasome inhibitors restores killing experimentally.

**Chloroquine resistance evolution.** PfCRT is a drug/metabolite transporter on the digestive vacuole membrane; the K76T substitution removes a positive charge, allowing the protonated drug to be transported out. Resistance spread from a few independent origins across continents. Notably, after chloroquine withdrawal in Malawi, susceptible parasites returned within about a decade because the mutant transporter carries a fitness cost, a rare example of reversible resistance.

**Hypnozoite pharmacology.** 8-aminoquinolines require metabolic activation by **CYP2D6** to hydroxylated metabolites that redox-cycle with NADPH:cytochrome P450 reductase, generating hydrogen peroxide. This shared mechanism explains both antirelapse efficacy and hemolysis in G6PD-deficient red cells, which cannot regenerate NADPH to maintain glutathione. Tafenoquine's very long half-life allows a single-administration radical cure but makes hemolysis prolonged if G6PD deficiency is missed, so quantitative G6PD testing is required.

**New directions:** ganaplacide (imidazolopiperazine) with lumefantrine, PfATP4 inhibitors (cipargamin), and monoclonal antibodies against the circumsporozoite protein for prevention, alongside the RTS,S and R21 vaccines.
levels.expert:
**Severe and cerebral malaria are emergencies.** Any fever in a traveler returning from an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise: thick and thin smears or a rapid diagnostic test immediately, repeated if negative. Severe falciparum malaria (impaired consciousness, seizures, severe anemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, renal failure, high parasitemia) requires **IV artesunate**, which reduced mortality compared with quinine in large trials (SEAQUAMAT in adults, AQUAMAT in children), followed by a full oral ACT course.

**Cerebral malaria for the neuro-minded:** parasitized red cells adhere to brain microvascular endothelium (PfEMP1 binding to EPCR and ICAM-1), causing microvascular obstruction, blood-brain barrier breakdown and brain swelling; in African children, MRI shows severe brain swelling associated with death. Management: artesunate, treat seizures, check glucose often (both disease and quinine cause hypoglycemia), avoid corticosteroids and mannitol (no benefit or harm in trials). Survivors, especially children, may have lasting cognitive deficits or epilepsy.

**Monitoring after artesunate:** check hemoglobin for **delayed hemolysis** in the weeks after treatment.

**Uncomplicated malaria:** an ACT appropriate to region; chloroquine only for species and regions with documented susceptibility. For *P. vivax* or *P. ovale*, add **primaquine or tafenoquine** for radical cure after **G6PD testing**, or relapses follow.

**Prophylaxis choices for travelers:** atovaquone-proguanil (well tolerated, short post-trip course), doxycycline (inexpensive, photosensitivity), mefloquine (convenient, but avoid with psychiatric or seizure history), tafenoquine (G6PD testing required). Mosquito avoidance (repellents, nets) remains essential because no regimen is perfect.

**Interactions and pitfalls:** QT-prolonging combinations (quinine, mefloquine, lumefantrine, piperaquine, plus other QT drugs); halofantrine is largely abandoned for cardiotoxicity; and chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine retinal screening for long-term rheumatology use.

keyPoints: Plasmodium: liver stage (hypnozoites in P. vivax/ovale) then blood stage (hemoglobin digestion, symptoms)
Chloroquine blocks heme detoxification into hemozoin; resistance via PfCRT
Artemisinins: endoperoxide activated by heme iron; fastest killers; used in ACTs; IV artesunate for severe malaria; kelch13 partial resistance
Primaquine/tafenoquine kill hypnozoites (radical cure) but cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Prophylaxis: atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine (neuropsychiatric effects)

lessons.title: Antihelminthics and Antiprotozoals

levels.kid:
**Worms** and tiny one-celled critters called **protozoa** can live inside people and make them sick.

Worm medicines often work by making the worm's muscles stop working, so it can't hold on and gets flushed out. Some freeze the worm stiff, others make it go floppy.

One worm, the pork tapeworm, can even make little cysts in the brain. Doctors use worm medicine plus medicine to calm swelling.

Other medicines fight protozoa, like the ones that cause sleeping sickness or bad tummy bugs. Each critter needs its own special medicine.
levels.hs:
**Helminths** (parasitic worms) and **protozoa** (single-celled parasites) cause huge amounts of disease worldwide.

**Antihelminthics** mostly target worm **nerves, muscles or cell structure**:
- **Albendazole and mebendazole** (benzimidazoles): bind worm **tubulin**, blocking microtubules so worms can't absorb glucose. Treat roundworm, hookworm, pinworm and **neurocysticercosis** (pork tapeworm cysts in the brain).
- **Ivermectin:** opens **chloride channels** in worm nerves and muscles, causing paralysis. Treats strongyloides, river blindness (onchocerciasis) and **scabies**. Mammals are protected because our brain's barrier pumps it out.
- **Praziquantel:** causes calcium to flood into flatworms (flukes and tapeworms), producing **spastic paralysis**. Treats **schistosomiasis** and tapeworms.
- **Pyrantel pamoate:** activates worm nicotinic receptors, paralyzing them (pinworm).

**Antiprotozoals:**
- **Metronidazole/tinidazole:** *Giardia*, amebic dysentery, *Trichomonas*.
- **Nitazoxanide:** *Cryptosporidium* and *Giardia*.
- **Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin:** **toxoplasmosis**, including brain infection in people with weak immunity.
- **Sleeping sickness** (*Trypanosoma brucei*): **fexinidazole** (oral) and **eflornithine**-based therapy; older drug melarsoprol is very toxic.
- **Chagas disease** (*T. cruzi*): benznidazole, nifurtimox.
- **Leishmaniasis:** liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine.
levels.college:
**Benzimidazoles (albendazole, mebendazole):** bind parasite **β-tubulin** (colchicine-site region) with far greater affinity than mammalian tubulin, inhibiting polymerization; impaired glucose uptake and vesicle transport cause slow death. Albendazole is absorbed better with a fatty meal and converted to the active **albendazole sulfoxide**; mebendazole acts mainly in the gut lumen. Uses: soil-transmitted helminths, pinworm, **neurocysticercosis**, echinococcosis (hydatid cysts, with surgery or PAIR). Adverse: GI upset, hepatitis and **bone marrow suppression** with prolonged courses, teratogenic in animals. Resistance in livestock nematodes via β-tubulin F200Y.

**Ivermectin (macrocyclic lactone):** potentiates/opens **glutamate-gated chloride channels** (GluCl) in invertebrate neurons and pharyngeal muscle, causing flaccid paralysis. Mammals lack GluCl; ivermectin binds mammalian GABA-A receptors but is excluded from the CNS by **P-glycoprotein** (dogs with MDR1 deletions, such as some collies, develop neurotoxicity). Uses: strongyloidiasis, onchocerciasis (kills microfilariae), scabies, lice. **Loa loa** coinfection with high microfilarial load risks **encephalopathy** from dying microfilariae.

**Praziquantel:** activates the flatworm transient receptor potential channel **TRPM_PZQ**, causing Ca²⁺ influx, sustained contraction and tegument vacuolization that exposes antigens to the host immune system. Uses: schistosomiasis, tapeworms, liver and lung flukes, neurocysticercosis. Metabolized by CYP3A4 (rifampin abolishes levels; dexamethasone reduces them).

**Pyrantel:** depolarizing nicotinic agonist (spastic paralysis). **Diethylcarbamazine:** lymphatic filariasis (Mazzotti reactions in onchocerciasis).

**Antiprotozoals:**
- **Nitazoxanide:** inhibits **PFOR**; Cryptosporidium, Giardia.
- **Entamoeba:** metronidazole for tissue invasion, then a **luminal agent** (paromomycin) to clear cysts.
- **Toxoplasma:** pyrimethamine (DHFR) + sulfadiazine (DHPS) + leucovorin.
- **Human African trypanosomiasis:** suramin (early *T. b. rhodesiense*), pentamidine (early *gambiense*), **melarsoprol** (arsenical; reactive encephalopathy), **eflornithine** (irreversible ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor; polyamine depletion) with nifurtimox (NECT), and **fexinidazole**, an oral nitroimidazole for both stages of *gambiense*.
- **Chagas:** benznidazole and nifurtimox (nitro-reduction by parasite type I nitroreductase).
- **Leishmaniasis:** liposomal amphotericin B, **miltefosine** (alkylphosphocholine, oral, teratogenic), pentavalent antimonials, paromomycin.
- **Free-living amoebae** (*Naegleria*, *Balamuthia*, *Acanthamoeba*): combinations including miltefosine, with very high mortality.
levels.phd:
**Neurocysticercosis pharmacology is immunology.** *Taenia solium* cysts in the brain evade immunity for years via immunomodulatory molecules. Antiparasitic treatment kills cysts, releasing antigens and triggering perilesional inflammation that can cause seizures, edema and raised intracranial pressure. Treatment decisions therefore weigh cyst stage: viable vesicular cysts benefit; calcified lesions (dead) do not need antiparasitics. Randomized trials (Garcia and colleagues) showed that albendazole combined with praziquantel improves cyst resolution in patients with multiple cysts versus albendazole alone, with corticosteroids given to blunt the inflammatory response. Dexamethasone and anticonvulsants interact pharmacokinetically: corticosteroids raise albendazole sulfoxide but lower praziquantel exposure, and enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs lower both.

**Molecular targets of old drugs revealed late.** Praziquantel's target remained unknown for four decades until Marchant and colleagues (2021) identified a schistosome TRPM channel whose activation by praziquantel accounts for its effects, and showed that structural variation in that channel explains species differences in sensitivity. Ivermectin's GluCl binding site lies between transmembrane helices at the subunit interface, stabilizing an open conformation, as shown by Hibbs and Gouaux's crystal structure of *C. elegans* GluClα (2011). Campbell and Ōmura shared the 2015 Nobel Prize for avermectin discovery alongside Tu Youyou.

**Trypanosome drug chemistry.** Eflornithine's selectivity rests on enzyme turnover: trypanosomal ornithine decarboxylase is stable while the human enzyme turns over in minutes, so irreversible inhibition depletes parasite polyamines and trypanothione (the parasite-specific thiol). Melarsoprol enters via the P2 aminopurine transporter and the aquaglyceroporin AQP2, whose loss confers cross-resistance with pentamidine. Nitro drugs (nifurtimox, benznidazole, fexinidazole) are activated by an oxygen-insensitive type I nitroreductase absent from mammals; its loss confers cross-resistance across the class.

**Toxoplasma latency.** Bradyzoite cysts in brain and muscle are not eradicated by current drugs, which act on tachyzoites; hence lifelong risk of reactivation under immunosuppression and the need for suppressive therapy until immune recovery.
levels.expert:
**Neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of acquired epilepsy in many low- and middle-income countries and a frequent neurosurgical problem.** Workup: MRI (scolex as a "dot" within a cyst) plus CT for calcifications, serology (EITB), and a fundoscopic exam for papilledema before antiparasitics. Key management principles:
- **Antiseizure medication** for patients with seizures.
- **Antiparasitic therapy** (albendazole, plus praziquantel when cysts are multiple) for viable parenchymal cysts, always with **corticosteroids** started beforehand.
- **Do not give antiparasitics with untreated raised intracranial pressure** or in cysticercal encephalitis (massive cyst burden), where inflammation could be fatal; treat the pressure first.
- **Intraventricular cysts** causing hydrocephalus are removed **endoscopically**, and shunting may be needed; subarachnoid (racemose) disease needs prolonged antiparasitic therapy and steroids.
- Screen household members for *T. solium* tapeworm carriage.
- Test for **Strongyloides** (or empirically treat with ivermectin) in patients from endemic areas before prolonged corticosteroids, because steroids can trigger fatal hyperinfection.

**Toxoplasma encephalitis** in advanced HIV: multiple ring-enhancing lesions; start pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-leucovorin (or TMP-SMX) and reassess imaging; failure to improve suggests lymphoma and the need for biopsy.

**Other practical points:**
- Ivermectin: check for *Loa loa* in patients from Central Africa before mass-type treatment.
- Praziquantel: avoid with rifampin; ocular cysticercosis must be excluded first because killing cysts in the eye can destroy vision.
- Amebic liver abscess: metronidazole then a luminal agent.
- Sleeping sickness: fexinidazole now avoids lumbar punctures and toxic arsenicals for many patients; staging still matters for the most severe cases.
- Primary amebic meningoencephalitis (*Naegleria*) is nearly always fatal; aggressive combinations including miltefosine, plus management of intracranial pressure, offer the only chance.

keyPoints: Benzimidazoles (albendazole, mebendazole) bind worm β-tubulin; used for roundworms and neurocysticercosis
Ivermectin opens invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels (flaccid paralysis); P-glycoprotein excludes it from the mammalian CNS
Praziquantel activates flatworm TRPM_PZQ → Ca²⁺ influx, spastic paralysis; schistosomes, tapeworms, flukes
Neurocysticercosis: antiparasitics plus corticosteroids and antiseizure drugs; treat raised ICP first; endoscopic removal for ventricular cysts
Protozoa: toxoplasma (pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin), trypanosomes (fexinidazole, eflornithine, melarsoprol), leishmania (liposomal amphotericin, miltefosine)
